text:
The air in Blackwood Bay had taken on a peculiar chill, not just the usual coastal damp, but something sharper, like a promise of withdrawal. It clung to the old timber storefronts, whispering through the skeletal branches of the pines. David Vance shivered, adjusting his worn trench coat collar. The static on the old radio in his office had worsened overnight, not just a hiss, but a low thrum that seemed to vibrate in the floorboards. He’d woken to it, a persistent hum that felt less like an electrical fault and more like the earth itself clearing its throat.

He ran a hand over the map tacked to his wall, the red circles marking the vanished. Three points, then four, now an unnerving seven scattered across the bay’s lonely stretches. Each disappearance a knot in the town’s frayed sanity. Earlier, Mrs. Gable, eyes wide and watery, had told him about the strange number painted on her barn door – a hastily scrawled ‘7773’. Not quite graffiti, not quite an accident. Just a number that felt too specific to be random, too out of place to ignore. He’d found another, almost identical, etched into the damp concrete near the abandoned lighthouse.

The low thrum persisted, an almost subsonic vibration that made the windows rattle faintly. The town’s old-timers mumbled about things pulling back, about the sky thinning. David didn't have much stock in omens, but Blackwood Bay had a way of blurring the lines between superstition and stark reality. And a journalist, even a jaded one like him, learned to pay attention when the world around him started speaking in riddles and numbers.
